title: Topology-guided rotational dynamics of magnetic soliton assemblies under pulsed current

paper_content.abstract:
Emergent topological spin textures, such as nanometric skyrmions and antiskyrmions, not
only exhibit a wealth of novel physical phenomena but also represent promising candidates for
next-generation spintronic devices due to their topological stability and low-current-driven
dynamics. Investigating their responses to electric currents is essential for uncovering unique
electromagnetic properties and advancing their integration into electronic technologies. While
considerable progress has been made through extensive research over the past decade, key
challenges still persist. In this study, we demonstrate the novel, current-driven oppositely rotating
dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in terms of Lorentz transmission electron
microscopy. Their senses of rotation are strongly dictated by their inherent topological charges and
remain largely unaffected by current direction, showing consistent behavior observed across
various sample geometries. Further experimental analyses have revealed a reduction in angular
velocity as (anti)skyrmions move away from the sample edge. The theoretical analyses, combined
with micromagnetic simulations, highlight the critical roles of boundary-induced confining
potentials and gyrotropic forces in steering the rotational dynamics of (anti)skyrmions. These
findings offer new insights into current-driven (anti)skyrmion dynamics and open promising
avenues for advancing topological concepts in confined spintronic systems.
paper_content.introduction:
Magnetic skyrmions, characterized by their vortex-like noncollinear spin configurations,
occupy an important position in contemporarNy condensed matter physics due to their unique
topological properties and promising funct ional applications1,2. Skyrmions are found in diverse
magnetic systems and exhibit sizes raLnging from nanometers to micrometers3-5. Their topological
charge Q is defined as Q = 1I ∬m(r)∙(∂ m(r)×∂ m(r))d2r, where m(r) is the unit vector of
4π x y
magnetization. The Q typically takes integer values of 1 for skyrmions, with the sign set by the
core polarity1,2. Investigating the dynamics of skyrmions is essential for gaining insight into their
intricate topological entities and extending their applicability6,7. The dynamics of skyrmions are
driven by various external stimuli, including magnetic fields8, electric/thermal currents9-14,
magnons15,16 and acoustic waves17. Among these, current-induced dynamics are particularly well-
regarded and have been intensively studied due to their operational simplicity and superior energy
efficiency. The dynamics of skyrmions under current flows can be described by the Thiele
equation18-20, in which the gyrotropic vector G = 4πQẑ originates from the topological properties
of skyrmions. As a consequence, current-driven skyrmions acquire a finite transverse velocity
component, known as the skyrmion Hall effect1,18-20. This intriguing phenomenon has been
observed in both multilayer systems12,13 and bulk samples14,21, emerging as a defining feature of
skyrmions.

In realistic systems, skyrmions inevitably experience boundary-induced confinement,
which can strongly modify their dynamics under electric current flows. The interplay between
gyrotropic forces and confining potentials leads to rich transport behaviors distinct from those in
unbounded media22-23, highlighting the importance of confinement effects for both fundamental
studies and technological implementations.

In contrast to the extensive progress made in theR study of skyrmions, the investigations of
antiskyrmions remain relatively limited. Antiskyrm ions are characterized by a topological charge
of opposite sign24 to that of skyrmions Iand have been demonstrated to form in non-
centrosymmetric magnetic systems with D or S symmetry25,26, where anisotropic
2d 4
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) give rise to complex spin textures27-29. Antiskyrmions
have been observed in Heusler compounds27,30 and schreibersite-type materials, including
(Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P (F A NPP)31-33, as well as in multilayer films34,35. While theoretical models
predict that the dynamics of antiskyrmions should mirror those of skyrmions with reversed
trajectories due to the sign reversal of the topological charge36, experimental validation is still
scarce. To date, only experimentally confirmed current-driven motion of antiskyrmions is their
constrained sliding along stripe domains33,37, offering limited insight into dynamics guided by
topological properties. More complex behaviors—such as rotational motion—have neither been
experimentally demonstrated nor systematically explored. This lack of experimental insight leaves
a critical gap in understanding the topological properties of antiskyrmion dynamics, underscoring
the need for further investigation.

In this study, through in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy (L-TEM), we have
identified novel current-induced rotations in skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies confined
within finite geometries. By altering the direction of the pulse current, we have demonstrated that
the consistent rotational dynamics of the assemblies are guided by their intrinsic topological
charges, independent of the current-flow orientation. The first experimental observation of current-
driven motion in antiskyrmion assemblies also validates the dynamic manifestation of its opposite
topology with skyrmions. Additionally, experimental observations in samples with different
geometries have confirmed that the rotation direction of (anti)skyrmions is independent of sample
geometry. In the circular shaped sample, the analyses Rof angular velocity across varying radial
distances have revealed a decrease in skyrmion velo city as they approach the center of the sample,
highlighting the significant impact of the bIoundary potential on rotational dynamics. Further
validation through micromagnetic simulations aligns with theoretical analyses, underscoring the
critical role of both the boundary and the gyrotropic force in governing skyrmion motion.
paper_content.results:
Unidirectional rotatAion of (anti)skyrmion assemblies driven by pulse currents
Here, to highlight the differences in in-plane magnetization configurations between
skyrmions and antiskyrmions, we describe skyrmion as vortex-like and antiskyrmion as
antivortex-like magnetization textures, extending beyond the definition solely on topological
charge. A comprehensive classification and detailed depiction of these unique spin configurations
are provided in Supplementary Fig. S1.

The in-situ L-TEM experiments were performed on FNPP samples. Figure 1a shows the
schematic of the rectangular sample we prepared via a dual-beam system composed of a Focused
Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) as detailed in the Methods section. The
view plane for L-TEM observation is the (001) and its edges aligned along the <110> to coincide
with the wavevectors of stripy structures33. The L-TEM image listed in Fig. 1b shows the diverse
topological spin textures under an applied magnetic field along −z direction in the fabricated
sample. Both rectangular antiskyrmions and elliptic skyrmions with opposite helicities31-33 can be
stabilized, attributed to the anisotropic DMI in FNPP. The transport-of-intensity equation (TIE)
analyses in Fig. 1c point out the configurations of the in-plane components of each spin textures,
consistent with the previous results28, 31-33.

Figure 1d and e represent schematic diagrams summarizing the in-situ measurements.
The skyrmion assemblies (Fig. 1d) or antiskyrmion assemRblies (Fig. 1e) are respectively stabilized
under the external field. As defined in Supplementa ry Note1, when the magnetic field B is applied
along the −z axis, the created skyrmion assemIblies possess a topological charge of Q = +1, while
the antiskyrmion assemblies possess Q = −1. Both skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies display
rotational dynamics under pulsed currents, yet rotating senses are opposite: counterclockwise
(CCW) for skyrmions (Fig. 1d), while clockwise (CW) for antiskyrmions (Fig. 1e) when the
external field is kept along the −z axis. Importantly, the current flows, whether along the +x or −x
axis, do not affect the direction of skyrmion/antiskyrmion rotations, highlighting that the senses of
rotation are highly related to the topological charge. Additionally, as shown in the schematics
(Fig.1), (anti)skyrmions located near the sample center show slower motions than those nearer the
sample boundary, illustrating the significant impact of boundary effects on their rotational
dynamics.

Sequential L-TEM observations of rotational motions of skyrmion assemblies
Figure 2 provides detailed visuals and descriptions according to the in-situ L-TEM
observations under current flows. Both the influence of topological charge and current polarity are
examined in this part. Figure 2a presents the L-TEM image of a stabilized antiskyrmion assembly
under a magnetic field of 518 mT along −z axis. Three representative antiskyrmions are highlighted
using arrows of different colors, and their initial positions are marked with dashed boxes to
facilitate motion tracking. The antiskyrmion assembly is robust and reproducible without
spontaneous annihilation or significant rearrangement during L-TEM imaging, indicating that the
ambient thermal fluctuations alone are insufficient to induce any observable dynamics such as
Brownian motion38,39 in the present experimental setup. Upon application of multiple pulsed
current with 20-ns width along +x direction, the antiskyrmion assembly exhibits a CW rotation
(Fig. 2a−c, also see in Supplementary video 1). Our expeRrimental results mark the first documented
instance of antiskyrmion rotation induced by pu lsed currents, establishing a novel mode for
antiskyrmion’s dynamic physics.

By adjusting the sample tilting conditions and magnetic field strength to 523 mT, a
skyrmion assembly with Q = +1 is also stabilized (Fig. 2d−f). To facilitate clearer tracking the
assembly, two skyrmions with opposite contrasts are deliberately marked in black and orange, as
shown in Fig. 2d. These skyrmions exhibit a CCW rotation under identical pulsed current
excitation and complete one full loop after several pulses (also see in Supplementary video 2),
clearly demonstrating dynamic behavior opposite to that of antiskyrmions. Remarkably, the
rotation of the skyrmion assembly remains CCW despite the current reversal (Fig. 2g−i, also see
in Supplementary video 3). In earlier studies, geometric confinement was exploited to cause the
skyrmion Hall motion into arc-shaped trajectories, and the sense of rotation was inferred from
multiple arc segments obtained by reversing the current polarity40. In contrast, the current
presentation not only represents the first experimental observation of complete current-driven
rotational motions of (anti)skyrmions but further demonstrates that the rotation of (anti)skyrmions
is independent of the current direction, which differs from skyrmion Hall motion influenced by
both current and temperature gradients41,42. Additional experiments with varying pulse widths
(Supplementary Fig. S2) show that excessively long pulses suppress the rotational motion due to
enhanced Joule heating. Accordingly, the 20-ns pulse width used in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 ensures
efficient current-driven excitation while minimizing thermal perturbations.

In addition, Supplementary Fig. S3 compares skyrmion assemblies stabilized under
opposite perpendicular magnetic fields (along the +z direction). As a result of the reversed field, the
skyrmions carry topological charges Q = −1, opposite to the case in Fig. 2d−f. Correspondingly,
the direction of rotation under pulsed current excitation iRs reversed to CW (see also Supplementary
video 4), confirming the critical role of topologic al charge. The striking contrast in rotational
direction between skyrmions and antiskyrmIions underscores a strong correlation between the
rotational dynamics and the intrinsic topological properties of these spin textures. These results
advance the understanding and exploitation of topologically guided rotational mechanisms,
providing a novel pathway for current-driven spin textures without relying on thermal gradients or
external magnetic fields. Meanwhile, this marks the first experimental observation of current-
driven motion of antiskyrmions associated with their topological properties. The motion, which is
opposite to that of skyrmions, reflects their contrasting topological intrinsics.

The effect of confinement potential on rotational dynamics
When pulsed currents were applied along the short axis of a rectangular sample (see
Supplementary Fig. S4), rotational dynamics of skyrmions were observed. To further investigate
the geometric effect on the observed dynamics, a circular sample was fabricated using FIB. The
SEM image (Fig. 3a) illustrates the structure, which consists of two tungsten electrode pads
connected to a central FNPP region encircled by a tungsten ring. A protective carbon layer was
also deposited on top to prevent the curtaining effect during FIB thinning processes43. Due to
geometric confinement, the skyrmions within the central FNPP region (outlined by a black dashed
line) arrange into a circular pattern when stabilized under a perpendicular magnetic field (Fig. 3b).
Upon subsequent application of a pulsed current through the tungsten pads, skyrmions exhibited
CCW rotation (Supplementary Fig. S5 and Supplementary Video 5), in accordance with
observations described in Fig. 2d−f, thus confirming that the rotation direction of topological spin
textures does not depend on sample geometry. COMSOL simulations, as detailed in the Methods
section, indicate that the current inhomogeneity and temperature gradient under pulsed currents
(Supplementary Fig. S6) are minimal and negligible forR the rotational dynamics.

The angular velocity, ω, of skyrmions was further quantitatively estimated at four
different radial distances (schematically depIicted in Fig. 3c). For each radial position, angular
velocities were extracted from three representative skyrmions. The results with varying current
density in Fig. 3d demonstrate a decreasing trend in ω when the skyrmions approach the sample
center, with ω finally dropping to 0. The error bars reflect the experimental uncertainties like
statistical uncertainty and local pinning effects. Owing to the small sample tilting angle (∼5
degrees) and minimal thickness variation (< 50 nm) in our experiment, their influence on the
extracted angular velocities is negligible. The representative skyrmion trajectories under the same
current conditions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S7. Such a spatially correlated trend is difficult
to reconcile with random pinning or homogeneous damping effects, which would not naturally
produce a well-defined radial dependence. Due to the spin tilting at the sample boundaries in the
DMI system, the skyrmions experience a repulsive confinement potential from the boundary1,22.
Since the boundary potential energy experienced by skyrmions also exhibits a similar decreasing
trend with reducing radial distance, this indicates that the rotational velocity is strongly influenced
by the boundary confinement potential. Additionally, the current-density dependence of ω is also
shown in Fig. 3e. The increase in ω with current density is consistent with previous current-driven
experiments on skyrmions21,44,45, further highlighting the importance of the STT effect in initiating
this rotational motion. The absence of measurable texture distortions and excitation timescales far
exceeding intrinsic relaxation times suggest that effective inertia plays a negligible role in the
present regime.

Theoretical analyses and simulation results
Previous theoretical studies have extensively eRxplored skyrmion dynamics in proximity
to sample boundaries22,23, highlighting the critica l influence of boundary interactions. In this
section, we have summarized numerical simIulation results designed to elucidate the rotational
behavior of skyrmions under currents in confined geometries. Initially, the current-driven
dynamics of a single-skyrmion system has been simulated. Following this, the simulations have
been carried out for two-skyrmion and further multi-skyrmion systems (Fig. 4; see also
Supplementary Fig. S8−10). Comprehensive theoretical discussions and detailed derivations
supporting these simulations are provided in Supplementary Note2.

The simulation starts from a single skyrmion with a topological charge of Q = +1, as
depicted in Fig. 4a, which is first subjected to a DC current. Figure 4b presents the trajectory of
the skyrmion driven by a DC current applied along the horizontal direction, with its initial position
located at the system center. Under this current flow, the skyrmion moved toward the boundary,
eventually stopped at an equilibrium position, tracing a partial circular path. Following this, the
current was turned off to observe the relaxation dynamics, depicted in Fig. 4c. Remarkably, both
the driven and relaxation stages exhibited consistent CCW rotation, as explained quantitatively by
the Thiele equation (Eq. (1), also detailed in Supplementary Note2 and Supplementary Video 6).
This directional rotational behavior arises from gyrotropic dynamics characterized by the vector

direction.

These results suggest that the continuous rotation of a skyrmion arises from repeated

relaxation cycle accumulates into a net rotational motion of a skyrmion.

The dynamics of skyrmion assemblies with a topological charge of Q = +1 under current

This

analysis agrees well with experimental results, revealing the validity and effectiveness of the
confinement-potential model adopted in this work.

To systematically examine the role of relaxation time, the pulse width was fixed at 500 ns
and the pulse interval was varied under continuous pulse trains. Representative frames extracted
from the recorded videos are shown in Supplementary Fig. S11. When the interval is 5 μs, the
rotational motions disappear, whereas the interval up to 10 μs restores pronounced rotational
dynamics. The results demonstrate that an adequate relaxation time is essential for enabling the
observed rotational motion, providing strong experimental support for our proposed excitation–
relaxation mechanism and theoretical framework.

To clarify the experimental and simulation results regarding skyrmion-assembly motion,
we provide a comprehensive theoretical derivation and validation based on the Thiele equation in
Supplementary Note2. Collectively, the theoretical analysis underscores three key conclusions: (i)
the direction of skyrmion rotational dynamics depends solely on the sign of the topological charge
Q, and is independent of current direction; (ii) the reRlaxation time between current pulses is
important for the continuous rotation and the nonlin ear boundary confinement potential constitutes
the primary driving force underlying thesIe rotational dynamics; and (iii) the equilibrium
established by skyrmion-skyrmion interactions leads to the gradual reduction in angular velocity
as skyrmion assemblies approach the sample center.

In conclusion, we have experimentally demonstrated novel current-induced rotational
dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies confined within samples with different
geometries. The in-situ L-TEM results have revealed that the sense of rotation depends solely on
the intrinsic topological charge. Notably, this first experimental observation of antiskyrmion
assembly dynamics has directly confirmed their contrasting topological nature relative to
skyrmions. Further analyses have identified clear evidence for a decrease in the angular velocity
of spin textures toward the sample center, underscoring the crucial effect of confinement potentials
caused by the sample boundary. Complementary micromagnetic simulations and theoretical
modeling have emphasized the decisive roles of the nonlinear boundary potential and the
gyrotropic force in driving these unique rotational dynamics of topological spin textures as a
transient phenomenon. These results offer significant advances in exploring skyrmion dynamics.

FNPP single crystals utilizing a FIB technique. The (001) plane was selected for the sample, with
the edges aligned along the <110> direction to align with the spiral wave vector q, optimizing the
observation of skyrmion dynamics. The dimensioRns of the rectangular samples were
approximately 6 µm in length, 4 µm in width, an d 160 nm in thickness. Additionally, a round-

circle encased by a tungsten ring. For preparation of the round-shaped sample, part of the ring
region was first removed by FIB milling, followed by tungsten deposition into the milled area. The
remaining FNPP in the ring region was then removed, leaving only the tungsten in that area. The
diameter of the inner FNPP circle was set to 6 µm, with a thickness of 160 nm.

L-TEM observations
The in-situ observations of skyrmions under pulsed current were conducted using JEM−2100 and
JEM−2800 microscopes (JEOL, Japan), equipped with a double-tilt current-capable holder (Fusion
Select, Protochips). In L-TEM, since the objective lens is essentially a strong electromagnetic lens
composed of current-carrying coils, the application of vertical magnetic fields was controlled by
adjusting the objective-lens current. For capturing L-TEM images with the magnetic field oriented
along the +z direction, the JEM−2800 microscope was utilized. Conversely, images with the
magnetic field applied along the −z direction were captured using the JEM−2100 microscope.
Pulsed voltages were generated using an arbitrary function generator (AFG31252, Tektronix,
USA), with each pulse manually triggered at intervals exceeding 0.1 seconds. To quantitatively
analyze the in-plane magnetic induction fields, the under- and over-focused L-TEM images were
processed using the QPt software package (HREM Co., Japan), based on the transport-of-intensity
equation.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this paper, the authors highlighted the critical influence of boundary induced confining potential and gyro tropic forces in steering the rotational dynamics of (anti)skyrmions. The experiments are carefully designed. The results are interesting. The rotational dynamics are intriguing. However, I strongly recommend the authors clarify the following.
1. In previous experimental work, the nonreciprocal transportation and circulation of skyrmions have been discussed in detail (Nano Letters 22 (23), 9638-9644, (2022)). The authors should clarify the improvements of the current work with those in the literature.
2. In this work, the (anti)skyrmions are driven by current pulse. It has been reported that Skyrmion Brownian dynamics also have similar behaviors (Applied physics letters, 117, 082402 (2020), Applied Physics Letters 119, 072402 (2021)). It is also well known that the Joule heating is evitable for current pulses. The authors should clarify the thermal effect, spin-transfer-torque, and boundary effects.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript by Z. Li et al reports current-driven rotational dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in confined geometries, observed via in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, and supported by micromagnetic simulations as well as Thiele-equation-based analysis. The authors demonstrate that the sense of rotation is determined solely by the sign of the topological charge, independent of current polarity and sample geometry, and attribute the phenomenon to the interplay between gyrotropic forces and boundary-induced confinement potentials. The work addresses an important and timely problem in skyrmionics, particularly given the scarcity of experimental studies on antiskyrmion dynamics. The experimental data are generally convincing, and the antiskyrmion results are potentially impactful.
However, for publication in Nature Communications, the manuscript requires substantial revision. Several claims are overstated, the physical interpretation lacks sufficient quantitative support, and key assumptions are not adequately justified. I therefore recommend a major revision. Below, I outline my concerns as major and minor points, all of which should be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
Major comments:
1. Conceptual framing: topology-governed dynamics
The central claim that the observed rotational dynamics are governed by topology is conceptually overstated. While the direction of rotation is indeed determined by the sign of the topological charge via the gyrotropic term, the presence and magnitude of the rotation clearly (to me) depend on the boundary-induced confinement potential. In the absence of confinement, the Thiele equation predicts a transverse deflection rather than sustained rotation. Throughout the manuscript, the authors frequently suggest that topology alone governs the dynamics, whereas both the experimental results and theoretical framework indicate that topology sets the chirality, not the dynamics itself. The authors should therefore explicitly distinguish between:
- topology determining the sense of rotation, and
- confinement providing the restoring force that enables rotational motion
Following that, the title, abstract, and conclusions should be softened accordingly.
2. Boundary confinement potential: origin and quantification
The boundary-induced confinement potential plays a central role in the interpretation of the manuscript, yet its physical origin and functional form are not sufficiently discussed. Several key questions remain unresolved, including whether the confinement is dominated by magnetostatic energy, DMI-induced edge canting, or effective pinning arising from thickness variations. The manuscript assumes a nonlinear confinement potential but does not experimentally extract or independently validate its radial dependence. Moreover, the comparison between the experimental angular velocity profiles (Fig. 3d) and the simulated results (Fig. 4d) remains largely qualitative, with noticeable discrepancies that are acknowledged but not adequately addressed. I therefore urge the authors to:
- Provide a clear physical discussion of the confinement mechanism in FNPP,
- Attempt a semi-quantitative extraction of the effective potential from experimental data, or explicitly state the limitations of the model and thereby point out the reasons for such quantitative mismatch
3. A key result of the study is that sustained rotation is observed only under pulsed current, whereas a DC current leads to a static equilibrium. Although this behavior is reproduced in the simulations, the underlying physical mechanism is not clarified. In particular, the possible roles of relaxation dynamics, effective inertia, or transient overshoot are not discussed. Moreover, the choice of pulse parameters (t₁, t₂, and their ratio) appears ad hoc, with no experimental investigation of alternative parameter regimes. The authors should therefore either provide a more detailed physical explanation of why pulsed excitation is essential, or clearly state this as an empirical observation limited to the explored parameter range.
4. The experimental observation of current-driven antiskyrmion rotation represents a major strength of the manuscript. However, although recent experimental reports on current-driven antiskyrmion motion (such as sliding or confined motion) are cited, they are not discussed in sufficient depth. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is fundamentally new relative to these prior works, whether it is the rotational motion itself, the topology-controlled chirality, a comparative assessment of mobility, or the use of pulsed-current operation.
5. The micromagnetic simulations employ a single-sublattice ferromagnetic LLG framework to model FNPP, a structurally and magnetically complex, anisotropic, multi-element system. However, the validity of this approximation, as well as its limitations, is not discussed. More importantly, thermal fluctuations are neglected, despite the experiments being conducted at room temperature. In addition, the asymmetric DMI term is introduced without explicitly relating it to the underlying symmetry. A more careful justification of the modelling assumptions used to explain the experimental observations is therefore needed.
6. There are also a few quantitative rigors of the experimental analysis, as listed below:
- Angular velocities are reported without error bars or uncertainty estimates
- The number of tracked skyrmions at each radial position is limited
- Possible systematic effects (projection in L-TEM, drift, defocus variation) are not discussed
At a minimum, the authors should comment on experimental uncertainties and the reproducibility of the results.
Minor comments:
1. The manuscript is a bit long, with repetitive background material that could be shortened.
2. Several grammatical issues and typographical errors remain (e.g. figure captions, plural agreement).
3. Some figure captions lack sufficient standalone clarity.
4. Data availability is stated, but no guidance is given on accessing raw L-TEM videos or tracking data.
5. The discussion of potential device implications remains speculative and could be better focused or shortened.
In summary, the manuscript presents high-quality experimental data and reports an important observation, particularly concerning antiskyrmion dynamics. Nevertheless, to meet the standards of Nature Communications, the authors need to address the points raised above. Once these issues are satisfactorily resolved, the work would represent a strong and impactful contribution to the field of topological spin textures and merit consideration for publication.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

## Abstract

Emergent topological spin textures, such as nanometric skyrmions and antiskyrmions, not
only exhibit a wealth of novel physical phenomena but also represent promising candidates for
next-generation spintronic devices due to their topological stability and low-current-driven
dynamics. Investigating their responses to electric currents is essential for uncovering unique
electromagnetic properties and advancing their integration into electronic technologies. While
considerable progress has been made through extensive research over the past decade, key
challenges still persist. In this study, we demonstrate the novel, current-driven oppositely rotating
dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in terms of Lorentz transmission electron
microscopy. Their senses of rotation are strongly dictated by their inherent topological charges and
remain largely unaffected by current direction, showing consistent behavior observed across
various sample geometries. Further experimental analyses have revealed a reduction in angular
velocity as (anti)skyrmions move away from the sample edge. The theoretical analyses, combined
with micromagnetic simulations, highlight the critical roles of boundary-induced confining
potentials and gyrotropic forces in steering the rotational dynamics of (anti)skyrmions. These
findings offer new insights into current-driven (anti)skyrmion dynamics and open promising
avenues for advancing topological concepts in confined spintronic systems.

---

## Introduction

Magnetic skyrmions, characterized by their vortex-like noncollinear spin configurations,
occupy an important position in contemporarNy condensed matter physics due to their unique
topological properties and promising funct ional applications1,2. Skyrmions are found in diverse
magnetic systems and exhibit sizes raLnging from nanometers to micrometers3-5. Their topological
charge Q is defined as Q = 1I ∬m(r)∙(∂ m(r)×∂ m(r))d2r, where m(r) is the unit vector of
4π x y
magnetization. The Q typically takes integer values of 1 for skyrmions, with the sign set by the
core polarity1,2. Investigating the dynamics of skyrmions is essential for gaining insight into their
intricate topological entities and extending their applicability6,7. The dynamics of skyrmions are
driven by various external stimuli, including magnetic fields8, electric/thermal currents9-14,
magnons15,16 and acoustic waves17. Among these, current-induced dynamics are particularly well-
regarded and have been intensively studied due to their operational simplicity and superior energy
efficiency. The dynamics of skyrmions under current flows can be described by the Thiele
equation18-20, in which the gyrotropic vector G = 4πQẑ originates from the topological properties
of skyrmions. As a consequence, current-driven skyrmions acquire a finite transverse velocity
component, known as the skyrmion Hall effect1,18-20. This intriguing phenomenon has been
observed in both multilayer systems12,13 and bulk samples14,21, emerging as a defining feature of
skyrmions.

In realistic systems, skyrmions inevitably experience boundary-induced confinement,
which can strongly modify their dynamics under electric current flows. The interplay between
gyrotropic forces and confining potentials leads to rich transport behaviors distinct from those in
unbounded media22-23, highlighting the importance of confinement effects for both fundamental
studies and technological implementations.

In contrast to the extensive progress made in theR study of skyrmions, the investigations of
antiskyrmions remain relatively limited. Antiskyrm ions are characterized by a topological charge
of opposite sign24 to that of skyrmions Iand have been demonstrated to form in non-
centrosymmetric magnetic systems with D or S symmetry25,26, where anisotropic
2d 4
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) give rise to complex spin textures27-29. Antiskyrmions
have been observed in Heusler compounds27,30 and schreibersite-type materials, including
(Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P (F A NPP)31-33, as well as in multilayer films34,35. While theoretical models
predict that the dynamics of antiskyrmions should mirror those of skyrmions with reversed
trajectories due to the sign reversal of the topological charge36, experimental validation is still
scarce. To date, only experimentally confirmed current-driven motion of antiskyrmions is their
constrained sliding along stripe domains33,37, offering limited insight into dynamics guided by
topological properties. More complex behaviors—such as rotational motion—have neither been
experimentally demonstrated nor systematically explored. This lack of experimental insight leaves
a critical gap in understanding the topological properties of antiskyrmion dynamics, underscoring
the need for further investigation.

In this study, through in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy (L-TEM), we have
identified novel current-induced rotations in skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies confined
within finite geometries. By altering the direction of the pulse current, we have demonstrated that
the consistent rotational dynamics of the assemblies are guided by their intrinsic topological
charges, independent of the current-flow orientation. The first experimental observation of current-
driven motion in antiskyrmion assemblies also validates the dynamic manifestation of its opposite
topology with skyrmions. Additionally, experimental observations in samples with different
geometries have confirmed that the rotation direction of (anti)skyrmions is independent of sample
geometry. In the circular shaped sample, the analyses Rof angular velocity across varying radial
distances have revealed a decrease in skyrmion velo city as they approach the center of the sample,
highlighting the significant impact of the bIoundary potential on rotational dynamics. Further
validation through micromagnetic simulations aligns with theoretical analyses, underscoring the
critical role of both the boundary and the gyrotropic force in governing skyrmion motion.

---

## Results

Unidirectional rotatAion of (anti)skyrmion assemblies driven by pulse currents
Here, to highlight the differences in in-plane magnetization configurations between
skyrmions and antiskyrmions, we describe skyrmion as vortex-like and antiskyrmion as
antivortex-like magnetization textures, extending beyond the definition solely on topological
charge. A comprehensive classification and detailed depiction of these unique spin configurations
are provided in Supplementary Fig. S1.

The in-situ L-TEM experiments were performed on FNPP samples. Figure 1a shows the
schematic of the rectangular sample we prepared via a dual-beam system composed of a Focused
Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) as detailed in the Methods section. The
view plane for L-TEM observation is the (001) and its edges aligned along the <110> to coincide
with the wavevectors of stripy structures33. The L-TEM image listed in Fig. 1b shows the diverse
topological spin textures under an applied magnetic field along −z direction in the fabricated
sample. Both rectangular antiskyrmions and elliptic skyrmions with opposite helicities31-33 can be
stabilized, attributed to the anisotropic DMI in FNPP. The transport-of-intensity equation (TIE)
analyses in Fig. 1c point out the configurations of the in-plane components of each spin textures,
consistent with the previous results28, 31-33.

Figure 1d and e represent schematic diagrams summarizing the in-situ measurements.
The skyrmion assemblies (Fig. 1d) or antiskyrmion assemRblies (Fig. 1e) are respectively stabilized
under the external field. As defined in Supplementa ry Note1, when the magnetic field B is applied
along the −z axis, the created skyrmion assemIblies possess a topological charge of Q = +1, while
the antiskyrmion assemblies possess Q = −1. Both skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies display
rotational dynamics under pulsed currents, yet rotating senses are opposite: counterclockwise
(CCW) for skyrmions (Fig. 1d), while clockwise (CW) for antiskyrmions (Fig. 1e) when the
external field is kept along the −z axis. Importantly, the current flows, whether along the +x or −x
axis, do not affect the direction of skyrmion/antiskyrmion rotations, highlighting that the senses of
rotation are highly related to the topological charge. Additionally, as shown in the schematics

sample boundary, illustrating the significant impact of boundary effects on their rotational
dynamics.

observations under current flows. Both the influence of topological charge and current polarity are
examined in this part. Figure 2a presents the L-TEM image of a stabilized antiskyrmion assembly
under a magnetic field of 518 mT along −z axis. Three representative antiskyrmions are highlighted

antiskyrmion’s dynamic physics.

By adjusting the sample tilting conditions and magnetic field strength to 523 mT, a
skyrmion assembly with Q = +1 is also stabilized (Fig. 2d−f). To facilitate clearer tracking the
assembly, two skyrmions with opposite contrasts are deliberately marked in black and orange, as

clearly demonstrating dynamic behavior opposite to that of antiskyrmions. Remarkably, the
rotation of the skyrmion assembly remains CCW despite the current reversal (Fig. 2g−i, also see
in Supplementary video 3). In earlier studies, geometric confinement was exploited to cause the
skyrmion Hall motion into arc-shaped trajectories, and the sense of rotation was inferred from
multiple arc segments obtained by reversing the current polarity40. In contrast, the current
presentation not only represents the first experimental observation of complete current-driven
rotational motions of (anti)skyrmions but further demonstrates that the rotation of (anti)skyrmions
is independent of the current direction, which differs from skyrmion Hall motion influenced by

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Z. Li et al reports current-driven rotational dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in confined geometries, observed via in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, and supported by micromagnetic simulations as well as Thiele-equation-based analysis. The authors demonstrate that the sense of rotation is determined solely by the sign of the topological charge, independent of current polarity and sample geometry, and attribute the phenomenon to the interplay between gyrotropic forces and boundary-induced confinement potentials. The work addresses an important and timely problem in skyrmionics, particularly given the scarcity of experimental studies on antiskyrmion dynamics. The experimental data are generally convincing, and the antiskyrmion results are potentially impactful.
However, for publication in Nature Communications, the manuscript requires substantial revision. Several claims are overstated, the physical interpretation lacks sufficient quantitative support, and key assumptions are not adequately justified. I therefore recommend a major revision. Below, I outline my concerns as major and minor points, all of which should be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
Major comments:
1. Conceptual framing: topology-governed dynamics
The central claim that the observed rotational dynamics are governed by topology is conceptually overstated. While the direction of rotation is indeed determined by the sign of the topological charge via the gyrotropic term, the presence and magnitude of the rotation clearly (to me) depend on the boundary-induced confinement potential. In the absence of confinement, the Thiele equation predicts a transverse deflection rather than sustained rotation. Throughout the manuscript, the authors frequently suggest that topology alone governs the dynamics, whereas both the experimental results and theoretical framework indicate that topology sets the chirality, not the dynamics itself. The authors should therefore explicitly distinguish between:
- topology determining the sense of rotation, and
- confinement providing the restoring force that enables rotational motion
Following that, the title, abstract, and conclusions should be softened accordingly.
2. Boundary confinement potential: origin and quantification
The boundary-induced confinement potential plays a central role in the interpretation of the manuscript, yet its physical origin and functional form are not sufficiently discussed. Several key questions remain unresolved, including whether the confinement is dominated by magnetostatic energy, DMI-induced edge canting, or effective pinning arising from thickness variations. The manuscript assumes a nonlinear confinement potential but does not experimentally extract or independently validate its radial dependence. Moreover, the comparison between the experimental angular velocity profiles (Fig. 3d) and the simulated results (Fig. 4d) remains largely qualitative, with noticeable discrepancies that are acknowledged but not adequately addressed. I therefore urge the authors to:
- Provide a clear physical discussion of the confinement mechanism in FNPP,
- Attempt a semi-quantitative extraction of the effective potential from experimental data, or explicitly state the limitations of the model and thereby point out the reasons for such quantitative mismatch
3. A key result of the study is that sustained rotation is observed only under pulsed current, whereas a DC current leads to a static equilibrium. Although this behavior is reproduced in the simulations, the underlying physical mechanism is not clarified. In particular, the possible roles of relaxation dynamics, effective inertia, or transient overshoot are not discussed. Moreover, the choice of pulse parameters (t₁, t₂, and their ratio) appears ad hoc, with no experimental investigation of alternative parameter regimes. The authors should therefore either provide a more detailed physical explanation of why pulsed excitation is essential, or clearly state this as an empirical observation limited to the explored parameter range.
4. The experimental observation of current-driven antiskyrmion rotation represents a major strength of the manuscript. However, although recent experimental reports on current-driven antiskyrmion motion (such as sliding or confined motion) are cited, they are not discussed in sufficient depth. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is fundamentally new relative to these prior works, whether it is the rotational motion itself, the topology-controlled chirality, a comparative assessment of mobility, or the use of pulsed-current operation.
5. The micromagnetic simulations employ a single-sublattice ferromagnetic LLG framework to model FNPP, a structurally and magnetically complex, anisotropic, multi-element system. However, the validity of this approximation, as well as its limitations, is not discussed. More importantly, thermal fluctuations are neglected, despite the experiments being conducted at room temperature. In addition, the asymmetric DMI term is introduced without explicitly relating it to the underlying symmetry. A more careful justification of the modelling assumptions used to explain the experimental observations is therefore needed.
6. There are also a few quantitative rigors of the experimental analysis, as listed below:
- Angular velocities are reported without error bars or uncertainty estimates
- The number of tracked skyrmions at each radial position is limited
- Possible systematic effects (projection in L-TEM, drift, defocus variation) are not discussed
At a minimum, the authors should comment on experimental uncertainties and the reproducibility of the results.
Minor comments:
1. The manuscript is a bit long, with repetitive background material that could be shortened.
2. Several grammatical issues and typographical errors remain (e.g. figure captions, plural agreement).
3. Some figure captions lack sufficient standalone clarity.
4. Data availability is stated, but no guidance is given on accessing raw L-TEM videos or tracking data.
5. The discussion of potential device implications remains speculative and could be better focused or shortened.
In summary, the manuscript presents high-quality experimental data and reports an important observation, particularly concerning antiskyrmion dynamics. Nevertheless, to meet the standards of Nature Communications, the authors need to address the points raised above. Once these issues are satisfactorily resolved, the work would represent a strong and impactful contribution to the field of topological spin textures and merit consideration for publication.

## Paper

## Abstract

Emergent topological spin textures, such as nanometric skyrmions and antiskyrmions, not
only exhibit a wealth of novel physical phenomena but also represent promising candidates for
next-generation spintronic devices due to their topological stability and low-current-driven
dynamics. Investigating their responses to electric currents is essential for uncovering unique
electromagnetic properties and advancing their integration into electronic technologies. While
considerable progress has been made through extensive research over the past decade, key
challenges still persist. In this study, we demonstrate the novel, current-driven oppositely rotating
dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in terms of Lorentz transmission electron
microscopy. Their senses of rotation are strongly dictated by their inherent topological charges and
remain largely unaffected by current direction, showing consistent behavior observed across
various sample geometries. Further experimental analyses have revealed a reduction in angular
velocity as (anti)skyrmions move away from the sample edge. The theoretical analyses, combined
with micromagnetic simulations, highlight the critical roles of boundary-induced confining
potentials and gyrotropic forces in steering the rotational dynamics of (anti)skyrmions. These
findings offer new insights into current-driven (anti)skyrmion dynamics and open promising
avenues for advancing topological concepts in confined spintronic systems.

---

## Introduction

Magnetic skyrmions, characterized by their vortex-like noncollinear spin configurations,
occupy an important position in contemporarNy condensed matter physics due to their unique
topological properties and promising funct ional applications1,2. Skyrmions are found in diverse
magnetic systems and exhibit sizes raLnging from nanometers to micrometers3-5. Their topological
charge Q is defined as Q = 1I ∬m(r)∙(∂ m(r)×∂ m(r))d2r, where m(r) is the unit vector of
4π x y
magnetization. The Q typically takes integer values of 1 for skyrmions, with the sign set by the
core polarity1,2. Investigating the dynamics of skyrmions is essential for gaining insight into their
intricate topological entities and extending their applicability6,7. The dynamics of skyrmions are
driven by various external stimuli, including magnetic fields8, electric/thermal currents9-14,
magnons15,16 and acoustic waves17. Among these, current-induced dynamics are particularly well-
regarded and have been intensively studied due to their operational simplicity and superior energy
efficiency. The dynamics of skyrmions under current flows can be described by the Thiele
equation18-20, in which the gyrotropic vector G = 4πQẑ originates from the topological properties
of skyrmions. As a consequence, current-driven skyrmions acquire a finite transverse velocity
component, known as the skyrmion Hall effect1,18-20. This intriguing phenomenon has been
observed in both multilayer systems12,13 and bulk samples14,21, emerging as a defining feature of
skyrmions.

In realistic systems, skyrmions inevitably experience boundary-induced confinement,
which can strongly modify their dynamics under electric current flows. The interplay between
gyrotropic forces and confining potentials leads to rich transport behaviors distinct from those in
unbounded media22-23, highlighting the importance of confinement effects for both fundamental
studies and technological implementations.

In contrast to the extensive progress made in theR study of skyrmions, the investigations of
antiskyrmions remain relatively limited. Antiskyrm ions are characterized by a topological charge
of opposite sign24 to that of skyrmions Iand have been demonstrated to form in non-
centrosymmetric magnetic systems with D or S symmetry25,26, where anisotropic
2d 4
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) give rise to complex spin textures27-29. Antiskyrmions
have been observed in Heusler compounds27,30 and schreibersite-type materials, including
(Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P (F A NPP)31-33, as well as in multilayer films34,35. While theoretical models
predict that the dynamics of antiskyrmions should mirror those of skyrmions with reversed
trajectories due to the sign reversal of the topological charge36, experimental validation is still
scarce. To date, only experimentally confirmed current-driven motion of antiskyrmions is their
constrained sliding along stripe domains33,37, offering limited insight into dynamics guided by
topological properties. More complex behaviors—such as rotational motion—have neither been
experimentally demonstrated nor systematically explored. This lack of experimental insight leaves
a critical gap in understanding the topological properties of antiskyrmion dynamics, underscoring
the need for further investigation.

In this study, through in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy (L-TEM), we have
identified novel current-induced rotations in skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies confined
within finite geometries. By altering the direction of the pulse current, we have demonstrated that
the consistent rotational dynamics of the assemblies are guided by their intrinsic topological
charges, independent of the current-flow orientation. The first experimental observation of current-
driven motion in antiskyrmion assemblies also validates the dynamic manifestation of its opposite
topology with skyrmions. Additionally, experimental observations in samples with different
geometries have confirmed that the rotation direction of (anti)skyrmions is independent of sample
geometry. In the circular shaped sample, the analyses Rof angular velocity across varying radial
distances have revealed a decrease in skyrmion velo city as they approach the center of the sample,
highlighting the significant impact of the bIoundary potential on rotational dynamics. Further
validation through micromagnetic simulations aligns with theoretical analyses, underscoring the
critical role of both the boundary and the gyrotropic force in governing skyrmion motion.

---

## Results

Unidirectional rotatAion of (anti)skyrmion assemblies driven by pulse currents
Here, to highlight the differences in in-plane magnetization configurations between
skyrmions and antiskyrmions, we describe skyrmion as vortex-like and antiskyrmion as
antivortex-like magnetization textures, extending beyond the definition solely on topological
charge. A comprehensive classification and detailed depiction of these unique spin configurations
are provided in Supplementary Fig. S1.

The in-situ L-TEM experiments were performed on FNPP samples. Figure 1a shows the
schematic of the rectangular sample we prepared via a dual-beam system composed of a Focused
Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) as detailed in the Methods section. The
view plane for L-TEM observation is the (001) and its edges aligned along the <110> to coincide
with the wavevectors of stripy structures33. The L-TEM image listed in Fig. 1b shows the diverse
topological spin textures under an applied magnetic field along −z direction in the fabricated
sample. Both rectangular antiskyrmions and elliptic skyrmions with opposite helicities31-33 can be
stabilized, attributed to the anisotropic DMI in FNPP. The transport-of-intensity equation (TIE)
analyses in Fig. 1c point out the configurations of the in-plane components of each spin textures,
consistent with the previous results28, 31-33.

Figure 1d and e represent schematic diagrams summarizing the in-situ measurements.
The skyrmion assemblies (Fig. 1d) or antiskyrmion assemRblies (Fig. 1e) are respectively stabilized
under the external field. As defined in Supplementa ry Note1, when the magnetic field B is applied
along the −z axis, the created skyrmion assemIblies possess a topological charge of Q = +1, while
the antiskyrmion assemblies possess Q = −1. Both skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies display
rotational dynamics under pulsed currents, yet rotating senses are opposite: counterclockwise
(CCW) for skyrmions (Fig. 1d), while clockwise (CW) for antiskyrmions (Fig. 1e) when the
external field is kept along the −z axis. Importantly, the current flows, whether along the +x or −x
axis, do not affect the direction of skyrmion/antiskyrmion rotations, highlighting that the senses of
rotation are highly related to the topological charge. Additionally, as shown in the schematics
(Fig.1), (anti)skyrmions located near the sample center show slower motions than those nearer the
sample boundary, illustrating the significant impact of boundary effects on their rotational
dynamics.

Sequential L-TEM observations of rotational motions of skyrmion assemblies
Figure 2 provides detailed visuals and descriptions according to the in-situ L-TEM
observations under current flows. Both the influence of topological charge and current polarity are
examined in this part. Figure 2a presents the L-TEM image of a stabilized antiskyrmion assembly
under a magnetic field of 518 mT along −z axis. Three representative antiskyrmions are highlighted
using arrows of different colors, and their initial positions are marked with dashed boxes to
facilitate motion tracking. The antiskyrmion assembly is robust and reproducible without
spontaneous annihilation or significant rearrangement during L-TEM imaging, indicating that the
ambient thermal fluctuations alone are insufficient to induce any observable dynamics such as
Brownian motion38,39 in the present experimental setup. Upon application of multiple pulsed
current with 20-ns width along +x direction, the antiskyrmion assembly exhibits a CW rotation
(Fig. 2a−c, also see in Supplementary video 1). Our expeRrimental results mark the first documented
instance of antiskyrmion rotation induced by pu lsed currents, establishing a novel mode for
antiskyrmion’s dynamic physics.

By adjusting the sample tilting conditions and magnetic field strength to 523 mT, a
skyrmion assembly with Q = +1 is also stabilized (Fig. 2d−f). To facilitate clearer tracking the
assembly, two skyrmions with opposite contrasts are deliberately marked in black and orange, as
shown in Fig. 2d. These skyrmions exhibit a CCW rotation under identical pulsed current
excitation and complete one full loop after several pulses (also see in Supplementary video 2),
clearly demonstrating dynamic behavior opposite to that of antiskyrmions. Remarkably, the
rotation of the skyrmion assembly remains CCW despite the current reversal (Fig. 2g−i, also see
in Supplementary video 3). In earlier studies, geometric confinement was exploited to cause the
skyrmion Hall motion into arc-shaped trajectories, and the sense of rotation was inferred from
multiple arc segments obtained by reversing the current polarity40. In contrast, the current
presentation not only represents the first experimental observation of complete current-driven
rotational motions of (anti)skyrmions but further demonstrates that the rotation of (anti)skyrmions
is independent of the current direction, which differs from skyrmion Hall motion influenced by
both current and temperature gradients41,42. Additional experiments with varying pulse widths
(Supplementary Fig. S2) show that excessively long pulses suppress the rotational motion due to
enhanced Joule heating. Accordingly, the 20-ns pulse width used in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 ensures
efficient current-driven excitation while minimizing thermal perturbations.

In addition, Supplementary Fig. S3 compares skyrmion assemblies stabilized under
opposite perpendicular magnetic fields (along the +z direction). As a result of the reversed field, the
skyrmions carry topological charges Q = −1, opposite to the case in Fig. 2d−f. Correspondingly,
the direction of rotation under pulsed current excitation iRs reversed to CW (see also Supplementary
video 4), confirming the critical role of topologic al charge. The striking contrast in rotational
direction between skyrmions and antiskyrmIions underscores a strong correlation between the
rotational dynamics and the intrinsic topological properties of these spin textures. These results
advance the understanding and exploitation of topologically guided rotational mechanisms,
providing a novel pathway for current-driven spin textures without relying on thermal gradients or
external magnetic fields. Meanwhile, this marks the first experimental observation of current-
driven motion of antiskyrmions associated with their topological properties. The motion, which is
opposite to that of skyrmions, reflects their contrasting topological intrinsics.

The effect of confinement potential on rotational dynamics
When pulsed currents were applied along the short axis of a rectangular sample (see
Supplementary Fig. S4), rotational dynamics of skyrmions were observed. To further investigate
the geometric effect on the observed dynamics, a circular sample was fabricated using FIB. The
SEM image (Fig. 3a) illustrates the structure, which consists of two tungsten electrode pads
connected to a central FNPP region encircled by a tungsten ring. A protective carbon layer was
also deposited on top to prevent the curtaining effect during FIB thinning processes43. Due to
geometric confinement, the skyrmions within the central FNPP region (outlined by a black dashed
line) arrange into a circular pattern when stabilized under a perpendicular magnetic field (Fig. 3b).
Upon subsequent application of a pulsed current through the tungsten pads, skyrmions exhibited
CCW rotation (Supplementary Fig. S5 and Supplementary Video 5), in accordance with
observations described in Fig. 2d−f, thus confirming that the rotation direction of topological spin
textures does not depend on sample geometry. COMSOL simulations, as detailed in the Methods
section, indicate that the current inhomogeneity and temperature gradient under pulsed currents
(Supplementary Fig. S6) are minimal and negligible forR the rotational dynamics.

The angular velocity, ω, of skyrmions was further quantitatively estimated at four
different radial distances (schematically depIicted in Fig. 3c). For each radial position, angular
velocities were extracted from three representative skyrmions. The results with varying current
density in Fig. 3d demonstrate a decreasing trend in ω when the skyrmions approach the sample
center, with ω finally dropping to 0. The error bars reflect the experimental uncertainties like
statistical uncertainty and local pinning effects. Owing to the small sample tilting angle (∼5
degrees) and minimal thickness variation (< 50 nm) in our experiment, their influence on the
extracted angular velocities is negligible. The representative skyrmion trajectories under the same
current conditions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S7. Such a spatially correlated trend is difficult

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Z. Li et al reports current-driven rotational dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in confined geometries, observed via in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, and supported by micromagnetic simulations as well as Thiele-equation-based analysis. The authors demonstrate that the sense of rotation is determined solely by the sign of the topological charge, independent of current polarity and sample geometry, and attribute the phenomenon to the interplay between gyrotropic forces and boundary-induced confinement potentials. The work addresses an important and timely problem in skyrmionics, particularly given the scarcity of experimental studies on antiskyrmion dynamics. The experimental data are generally convincing, and the antiskyrmion results are potentially impactful.
However, for publication in Nature Communications, the manuscript requires substantial revision. Several claims are overstated, the physical interpretation lacks sufficient quantitative support, and key assumptions are not adequately justified. I therefore recommend a major revision. Below, I outline my concerns as major and minor points, all of which should be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
Major comments:
1. Conceptual framing: topology-governed dynamics
The central claim that the observed rotational dynamics are governed by topology is conceptually overstated. While the direction of rotation is indeed determined by the sign of the topological charge via the gyrotropic term, the presence and magnitude of the rotation clearly (to me) depend on the boundary-induced confinement potential. In the absence of confinement, the Thiele equation predicts a transverse deflection rather than sustained rotation. Throughout the manuscript, the authors frequently suggest that topology alone governs the dynamics, whereas both the experimental results and theoretical framework indicate that topology sets the chirality, not the dynamics itself. The authors should therefore explicitly distinguish between:
- topology determining the sense of rotation, and
- confinement providing the restoring force that enables rotational motion
Following that, the title, abstract, and conclusions should be softened accordingly.
2. Boundary confinement potential: origin and quantification
The boundary-induced confinement potential plays a central role in the interpretation of the manuscript, yet its physical origin and functional form are not sufficiently discussed. Several key questions remain unresolved, including whether the confinement is dominated by magnetostatic energy, DMI-induced edge canting, or effective pinning arising from thickness variations. The manuscript assumes a nonlinear confinement potential but does not experimentally extract or independently validate its radial dependence. Moreover, the comparison between the experimental angular velocity profiles (Fig. 3d) and the simulated results (Fig. 4d) remains largely qualitative, with noticeable discrepancies that are acknowledged but not adequately addressed. I therefore urge the authors to:
- Provide a clear physical discussion of the confinement mechanism in FNPP,
- Attempt a semi-quantitative extraction of the effective potential from experimental data, or explicitly state the limitations of the model and thereby point out the reasons for such quantitative mismatch
3. A key result of the study is that sustained rotation is observed only under pulsed current, whereas a DC current leads to a static equilibrium. Although this behavior is reproduced in the simulations, the underlying physical mechanism is not clarified. In particular, the possible roles of relaxation dynamics, effective inertia, or transient overshoot are not discussed. Moreover, the choice of pulse parameters (t₁, t₂, and their ratio) appears ad hoc, with no experimental investigation of alternative parameter regimes. The authors should therefore either provide a more detailed physical explanation of why pulsed excitation is essential, or clearly state this as an empirical observation limited to the explored parameter range.
4. The experimental observation of current-driven antiskyrmion rotation represents a major strength of the manuscript. However, although recent experimental reports on current-driven antiskyrmion motion (such as sliding or confined motion) are cited, they are not discussed in sufficient depth. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is fundamentally new relative to these prior works, whether it is the rotational motion itself, the topology-controlled chirality, a comparative assessment of mobility, or the use of pulsed-current operation.
5. The micromagnetic simulations employ a single-sublattice ferromagnetic LLG framework to model FNPP, a structurally and magnetically complex, anisotropic, multi-element system. However, the validity of this approximation, as well as its limitations, is not discussed. More importantly, thermal fluctuations are neglected, despite the experiments being conducted at room temperature. In addition, the asymmetric DMI term is introduced without explicitly relating it to the underlying symmetry. A more careful justification of the modelling assumptions used to explain the experimental observations is therefore needed.
6. There are also a few quantitative rigors of the experimental analysis, as listed below:
- Angular velocities are reported without error bars or uncertainty estimates
- The number of tracked skyrmions at each radial position is limited
- Possible systematic effects (projection in L-TEM, drift, defocus variation) are not discussed
At a minimum, the authors should comment on experimental uncertainties and the reproducibility of the results.
Minor comments:
1. The manuscript is a bit long, with repetitive background material that could be shortened.
2. Several grammatical issues and typographical errors remain (e.g. figure captions, plural agreement).
3. Some figure captions lack sufficient standalone clarity.
4. Data availability is stated, but no guidance is given on accessing raw L-TEM videos or tracking data.
5. The discussion of potential device implications remains speculative and could be better focused or shortened.
In summary, the manuscript presents high-quality experimental data and reports an important observation, particularly concerning antiskyrmion dynamics. Nevertheless, to meet the standards of Nature Communications, the authors need to address the points raised above. Once these issues are satisfactorily resolved, the work would represent a strong and impactful contribution to the field of topological spin textures and merit consideration for publication.

Comment 1. Conceptual framing: topology-governed dynamics

conceptually overstated. While the direction of rotation is indeed determined by the
sign of the topological charge via the gyrotropic term, the presence and magnitude of
the rotation clearly (to me) depend on the boundary-induced confinement potential. In
the absence of confinement, the Thiele equation predicts a transverse deflection rather
than sustained rotation. Throughout the manuscript, the authors frequently suggest that
topology alone governs the dynamics, whereas both the experimental results and
theoretical framework indicate that topology sets the chirality, not the dynamics itself.

- topology determining the sense of rotation, and
- confinement providing the restoring force that enables rotational motion

of the manuscript, yet its physical origin and functional form are not sufficiently
discussed. Several key questions remain unresolved, including whether the
confinement is dominated by magnetostatic energy, DMI-induced edge canting, or
effective pinning arising from thickness variations. The manuscript assumes a nonlinear
confinement potential but does not experimentally extract or independently validate its
radial dependence. Moreover, the comparison between the experimental angular
velocity profiles (Fig. 3d) and the simulated results (Fig. 4d) remains largely qualitative,

therefore urge the authors to:

- Provide a clear physical discussion of the confinement mechanism in FNPP,

exchange interaction between the skyrmion and the boundary-induced tilting generates

interaction. The competition between these two effects gives rise to an effective

repulsive interaction between skyrmions and the sample boundary, indicating that the

“Due to the spin tilting at the sample boundaries in the DMI system, the skyrmions

transverse velocity component and a finite angular displacement, which accumulates

micromagnetic simulations (Extended Data Fig. 7–8) and analytical treatment based on
the Thiele equation (Supplementary Note 2). The essential role of relaxation time has
been clarified in the revised main text (see line 286-291 in the revised manuscript), as
described below:
“These results suggest that the continuous rotation of a skyrmion arises from

“Additional experiments with varying pulse widths (Extended Data Fig. 1) show

Comment 4. The experimental observation of current-driven antiskyrmion rotation
represents a major strength of the manuscript. However, although recent experimental
reports on current-driven antiskyrmion motion (such as sliding or confined motion)
are cited, they are not discussed in sufficient depth. The manuscript would benefit from a

Response 4: We thank the referee for raising this important point regarding the
11

antiskyrmion dynamics, the reported motion has been largely limited to constrained
sliding along helical domains. In such scenarios, the motion is highly restricted and
exhibits limited characteristic topological signatures, such as Hall-like transverse
deflection. Consequently, no experimental evidence has been provided to directly
demonstrate the topological contrast between antiskyrmions and skyrmions through
their dynamics, let alone more complex motion modes.
In contrast, the present work reports the first real-space experimental observation
of rotational dynamics in antiskyrmion assemblies driven by electric current. This
rotation represents a qualitatively new dynamical regime that goes beyond confined
translational motion and is also highly related to its topological properties. More
importantly, we demonstrate that antiskyrmions rotate opposite to skyrmions under
identical excitation, providing the first dynamic experimental confirmation of their
opposite topological charges. This topology-dependent contrast cannot be inferred from
stripe-confined sliding motion alone and has not been experimentally established in
prior studies.
Therefore, the key novelty of our work lies in revealing a previously unobserved
topology-controlled rotational sense of antiskyrmion dynamics and establishing a direct
link between their motion and intrinsic topological properties. This extends current-

## Abstract

Emergent topological spin textures, such as nanometric skyrmions and antiskyrmions, not
only exhibit a wealth of novel physical phenomena but also represent promising candidates for
next-generation spintronic devices due to their topological stability and low-current-driven
dynamics. Investigating their responses to electric currents is essential for uncovering unique
electromagnetic properties and advancing their integration into electronic technologies. While
considerable progress has been made through extensive research over the past decade, key
challenges still persist. In this study, we demonstrate the novel, current-driven oppositely rotating
dynamics of skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies in terms of Lorentz transmission electron
microscopy. Their senses of rotation are strongly dictated by their inherent topological charges and
remain largely unaffected by current direction, showing consistent behavior observed across
various sample geometries. Further experimental analyses have revealed a reduction in angular
velocity as (anti)skyrmions move away from the sample edge. The theoretical analyses, combined
with micromagnetic simulations, highlight the critical roles of boundary-induced confining
potentials and gyrotropic forces in steering the rotational dynamics of (anti)skyrmions. These
findings offer new insights into current-driven (anti)skyrmion dynamics and open promising

## Introduction

Magnetic skyrmions, characterized by their vortex-like noncollinear spin configurations,
occupy an important position in contemporarNy condensed matter physics due to their unique
topological properties and promising funct ional applications1,2. Skyrmions are found in diverse
magnetic systems and exhibit sizes raLnging from nanometers to micrometers3-5. Their topological
charge Q is defined as Q = 1I ∬m(r)∙(∂ m(r)×∂ m(r))d2r, where m(r) is the unit vector of
4π x y
magnetization. The Q typically takes integer values of 1 for skyrmions, with the sign set by the
core polarity1,2. Investigating the dynamics of skyrmions is essential for gaining insight into their
intricate topological entities and extending their applicability6,7. The dynamics of skyrmions are
driven by various external stimuli, including magnetic fields8, electric/thermal currents9-14,
magnons15,16 and acoustic waves17. Among these, current-induced dynamics are particularly well-
regarded and have been intensively studied due to their operational simplicity and superior energy
efficiency. The dynamics of skyrmions under current flows can be described by the Thiele
equation18-20, in which the gyrotropic vector G = 4πQẑ originates from the topological properties
of skyrmions. As a consequence, current-driven skyrmions acquire a finite transverse velocity
component, known as the skyrmion Hall effect1,18-20. This intriguing phenomenon has been
observed in both multilayer systems12,13 and bulk samples14,21, emerging as a defining feature of
skyrmions.

In realistic systems, skyrmions inevitably experience boundary-induced confinement,
which can strongly modify their dynamics under electric current flows. The interplay between
gyrotropic forces and confining potentials leads to rich transport behaviors distinct from those in
unbounded media22-23, highlighting the importance of confinement effects for both fundamental
studies and technological implementations.

In contrast to the extensive progress made in theR study of skyrmions, the investigations of
antiskyrmions remain relatively limited. Antiskyrm ions are characterized by a topological charge
of opposite sign24 to that of skyrmions Iand have been demonstrated to form in non-
centrosymmetric magnetic systems with D or S symmetry25,26, where anisotropic
2d 4
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) give rise to complex spin textures27-29. Antiskyrmions
have been observed in Heusler compounds27,30 and schreibersite-type materials, including
(Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P (F A NPP)31-33, as well as in multilayer films34,35. While theoretical models
predict that the dynamics of antiskyrmions should mirror those of skyrmions with reversed
trajectories due to the sign reversal of the topological charge36, experimental validation is still
scarce. To date, only experimentally confirmed current-driven motion of antiskyrmions is their
constrained sliding along stripe domains33,37, offering limited insight into dynamics guided by
topological properties. More complex behaviors—such as rotational motion—have neither been
experimentally demonstrated nor systematically explored. This lack of experimental insight leaves
a critical gap in understanding the topological properties of antiskyrmion dynamics, underscoring
the need for further investigation.

In this study, through in-situ Lorentz transmission electron microscopy (L-TEM), we have
identified novel current-induced rotations in skyrmion and antiskyrmion assemblies confined
within finite geometries. By altering the direction of the pulse current, we have demonstrated that
the consistent rotational dynamics of the assemblies are guided by their intrinsic topological
charges, independent of the current-flow orientation. The first experimental observation of current-
driven motion in antiskyrmion assemblies also validates the dynamic manifestation of its opposite
topology with skyrmions. Additionally, experimental observations in samples with different
geometries have confirmed that the rotation direction of (anti)skyrmions is independent of sample
geometry. In the circular shaped sample, the analyses Rof angular velocity across varying radial
distances have revealed a decrease in skyrmion velo city as they approach the center of the sample,
highlighting the significant impact of the bIoundary potential on rotational dynamics. Further
validation through micromagnetic simulations aligns with theoretical analyses, underscoring the
critical role of both the boundary and the gyrotropic force in governing skyrmion motion.

## Results

Unidirectional rotatAion of (anti)skyrmion assemblies driven by pulse currents
Here, to highlight the differences in in-plane magnetization configurations between
skyrmions and antiskyrmions, we describe skyrmion as vortex-like and antiskyrmion as
antivortex-like magnetization textures, extending beyond the definition solely on topological
charge. A comprehensive classification and detailed depiction of these unique spin configurations
are provided in Supplementary Fig. S1.

The in-situ L-TEM experiments were performed on FNPP samples. Figure 1a shows the
schematic of the rectangular sample we prepared via a dual-beam system composed of a Focused
Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) as detailed in the Methods section. The
view plane for L-TEM observation is the (001) and its edges aligned along the <110> to coincide
with the wavevectors of stripy structures33. The L-TEM image listed in Fig. 1b shows the diverse
topological spin textures under an applied magnetic field along −z direction in the fabricated
sample. Both rectangular antiskyrmions and elliptic skyrmions with opposite helicities31-33 can be
